title: Analyze an Issue
lines: ## What you see on screen

The Analytical Writing section of the shorter GRE has one task: Analyze an Issue, with 30 minutes. The screen shows a short statement on a general topic (education, technology, the arts, government, science, work) followed by a specific set of instructions. Below it is a plain text box. You can type, delete, cut, copy, paste and undo, but there is no spell-check and no grammar check, so you must catch your own typing errors.
The statement is deliberately arguable. There is no correct position. The readers want to see how well you reason, support your view, and write clearly.
## The instructions matter

Each prompt comes with one instruction, and your essay must follow it. The instructions vary. Some ask you to say how far you agree or disagree and to consider ways the statement might or might not hold true. Others ask you to address the strongest objections to your view, to weigh two competing positions, to discuss the consequences of adopting a policy, or to consider specific situations in which a recommendation would or would not be wise.

! Read the instruction twice before planning. An essay that argues well but ignores the instruction (for example, never addressing counterarguments when asked to) will lose points no matter how polished it is.
## How the essay is scored

Your essay is scored on a scale from 0 to 6 in half-point steps. One trained human reader and a scoring program each evaluate it, and a second human reader is brought in if they disagree too much. Readers judge the essay as a whole, as a first draft written under time pressure, so a few typing slips will not sink a strong essay. In plain terms, the levels look like this:

- 6: A clear, insightful position, developed with persuasive reasons and well-chosen examples. The essay follows the instruction closely, is well organized with smooth transitions, and uses precise, varied language with very few errors.

- 5: A thoughtful, well-supported position that follows the instruction. Organization is clear and the language is good, though the analysis is a little less deep or the examples a little less sharp than at 6.
- 4: A clear position with relevant support, adequately organized. Development may be uneven, and there may be some errors, but meaning is clear.
- 3: Some competence but obvious weakness: vague or limited support, a weak link to the instruction, poor organization, or frequent errors that sometimes blur meaning.
- 2: Serious problems: little relevant reasoning, very weak organization, or errors that often make the writing hard to follow.
- 1: Fundamental deficiencies: very little coherent writing or almost no understanding of the task.
- 0: Off topic, copied from the prompt, in a language other than English, or blank.

What moves an essay up the scale is mostly the quality of thinking: a nuanced position, reasons that actually connect to the claim, and examples that are explained rather than merely mentioned. Length helps only when it adds development.
## A 30-minute plan

- Minutes 0 to 5, plan: Read the statement and instruction twice. Decide your position. List two or three reasons and an example for each. Note the strongest objection to your view and how you will answer it.

- Minutes 5 to 27, write: Introduction (about 3 minutes), two or three body paragraphs (about 5 minutes each), a paragraph on the counterargument if the instruction calls for it or if you have time, and a short conclusion (about 2 minutes).
- Minutes 27 to 30, proofread: Read once, quickly, for missing words, wrong words (their and there, its and it's), and sentences you meant to finish but did not.
! Do not skip the plan to "save time". Five minutes of planning is what lets you write for 22 minutes without stopping to wonder what comes next.
## A reusable structure
A clear essay of four or five paragraphs works for almost every prompt. Typical scoring essays run about 450 to 650 words.

- Introduction (3 to 4 sentences): Show you understand the issue, state your position with any limits, and preview your reasons. A qualified position ("largely true, but only when ...") is often more insightful than total agreement.
- Body paragraph 1: Your strongest reason. Topic sentence, then an example, then two or three sentences explaining how the example supports the reason.
- Body paragraph 2: A second, distinct reason, built the same way. Make sure it is not the first reason in new words.
- Body paragraph 3: The counterargument. State the best objection fairly, then explain why it does not overturn your view, or show the conditions under which it is right.
- Conclusion (2 to 3 sentences): Restate your position in fresh words and say what the discussion shows. Do not add a new argument here.
> Sample statement: Governments should fund scientific research only when it promises practical benefits.

> Sample instruction: Write a response in which you discuss the extent to which you agree or disagree with the recommendation, and explain how the circumstances in which adopting it would or would not be advantageous shape your position.

> A sample thesis: Requiring every publicly funded project to promise practical benefits sounds prudent, but it would misjudge how discoveries actually happen; a sensible policy funds applied work generously while protecting a share of research whose uses cannot yet be foreseen.

> Reasons in the plan: (1) many useful technologies grew from research with no practical aim at the start; (2) predicting "practical benefit" in advance is unreliable and favors safe, incremental projects; (3) counterargument: public money is limited and taxpayers deserve accountability; answer: accountability can be built into basic research through peer review and periodic evaluation, without demanding immediate payoffs.
Notice that the thesis is not simply "I disagree". It takes a position and states the circumstances, which is exactly what this instruction asks for.
## Developing examples
Examples are where most essays win or lose points. Readers do not reward obscure facts; they reward examples that are relevant, specific and explained.

- Use a mix of sources: history, science, business, the arts, education, and your own observation. A well-explained personal or hypothetical example is acceptable, though broad, widely understood examples usually persuade better.
- Be specific: "a regional hospital that cut its administrative staff to save money and then saw waiting times grow" is stronger than "many organizations".
- Explain the link: after every example, write one or two sentences saying exactly how it supports your reason. An example without explanation is just a story.
- Avoid invented statistics. Do not make up precise numbers or quotations and present them as fact. A clearly framed hypothetical ("Imagine a city that ...") is honest and fine.
> Weak: For example, the internet was invented by scientists. This shows research is good.

> Stronger: Much of the early networking research that later made the internet possible was funded to solve narrow problems of connecting computers between institutions, not to transform daily life. Had funders demanded a clear commercial use at the outset, it is hard to imagine anyone predicting online shopping or video calls. The example suggests that the most valuable benefits of research are often the ones no one could have listed in a funding application.
## Common mistakes
! Ignoring the instruction. Each instruction asks for something specific; build at least one paragraph around it.
! Sitting on the fence. Discussing both sides is good, but you must still reach a clear position.
! Listing examples without analysis. Three examples with no explanation are weaker than one example that is fully developed.
! Repeating the same reason in two paragraphs. Check in your plan that each body paragraph makes a different point.
! Running out of time without a conclusion. If you are at minute 26, write two sentences of conclusion immediately, then proofread.
! Relying on spell-check habits. The test editor has none. Choose words you can spell, and use your three proofreading minutes.
! Memorizing a whole essay. Readers recognize prepared, generic text that does not respond to the prompt, and it scores poorly. Prepare a structure and a bank of example areas, not sentences.
## Language that helps

Use transitions that show logic, not only sequence: however, as a result, by contrast, for this reason, admittedly, even so, in such cases. Vary your sentence length. Prefer precise, plain words to impressive vocabulary you might misuse. Short paragraphs with clear topic sentences make your organization easy to see.
## Quick checklist
- Did I follow the specific instruction?
- Is my position clear in the introduction, with its limits stated?
- Does each body paragraph have one distinct reason and a developed, explained example?
- Did I address a counterargument fairly?
- Did I leave three minutes to proofread without spell-check?
